claim: Mammalian brains are composed of many millions of neurons in mice.
source: While mammalian brains are composed of many millions (Herculano-Houzel et al., 2006) or billions (Herculano-Houzel, 2009; Herculano-Houzel et al., 2007) of neurons
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Herculano-Houzel et al., 2006.

claim: Mammalian brains are composed of billions of neurons in humans.
source: While mammalian brains are composed of many millions (Herculano-Houzel et al., 2006) or billions (Herculano-Houzel, 2009; Herculano-Houzel et al., 2007) of neurons
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Herculano-Houzel, 2009 and Herculano-Houzel et al., 2007.

claim: Brains operate through the activity of small subsets of neurons.
source: it has long been postulated that they operate – encoding information and controlling behaviour – through the activity of small subsets of those neurons (Barlow, 1972).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Barlow, 1972.

claim: The sparse coding hypothesis is supported computationally.
source: Indeed, the hypothesis that brains use sparse, distributed activity patterns is supported computationally (Kanerva, 1993; Olshausen and Field, 1996)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kanerva, 1993 and Olshausen and Field, 1996.

claim: The sparse coding hypothesis is supported energetically.
source: Indeed, the hypothesis that brains use sparse, distributed activity patterns is supported computationally (Kanerva, 1993; Olshausen and Field, 1996), energetically (Attwell and Laughlin, 2001; Lennie, 2003; Schölvinck et al., 2008)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Attwell and Laughlin, 2001; Lennie, 2003; Schölvinck et al., 2008.

claim: The sparse coding hypothesis is supported experimentally.
source: Indeed, the hypothesis that brains use sparse, distributed activity patterns is supported computationally (Kanerva, 1993; Olshausen and Field, 1996), energetically (Attwell and Laughlin, 2001; Lennie, 2003; Schölvinck et al., 2008), and experimentally (Barth and Poulet, 2012; Olshausen and Field, 2004; Wolfe et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Barth and Poulet, 2012; Olshausen and Field, 2004; Wolfe et al., 2010.

claim: Neuronal inhibition is thought to govern sparse coding.
source: A major factor thought to govern such sparse coding is neuronal inhibition (Haider and McCormick, 2009; Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Haider and McCormick, 2009; Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011.

claim: Neuronal inhibition serves to balance and control recurrent excitation.
source: which serves to balance and control recurrent excitation (Denève and Machens, 2016; Haider et al., 2013; Murphy and Miller, 2009; Packer and Yuste, 2011; Pehlevan and Sompolinsky, 2014; Sadeh and Clopath, 2020; Tsodyks et al., 1997; van Vreeswijk and Sompolinsky, 1996; Wehr and Zador, 2003; Wolf et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Neuronal inhibition shapes neuronal output.
source: and shape neuronal output (Borg-Graham et al., 1998; Cardin et al., 2010; Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011; Lee et al., 2012; Wilson et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Borg-Graham et al., 1998; Cardin et al., 2010; Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011; Lee et al., 2012; Wilson et al., 2012.

claim: Focal activation of cortical regions can influence decision-making.
source: Classical microstimulation experiments have demonstrated that focal activation of cortical regions can influence decision-making, providing a direct causal link between neural activity and behaviour (Cohen and Newsome, 2004; Murasugi et al., 1993; Salzman et al., 1990; Salzman et al., 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cohen and Newsome, 2004; Murasugi et al., 1993; Salzman et al., 1990; Salzman et al., 1992.

claim: Optogenetic activation of dozens to hundreds of cortical neurons can be directly detected.
source: This landmark work has been complemented by more recent studies showing that optogenetic activation of dozens to hundreds of cortical neurons can be directly detected (Huber et al., 2008; Histed and Maunsell, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Huber et al., 2008; Histed and Maunsell, 2014.

claim: Strong electrical stimulation of a single neuron can be detected in a cell-type and spike timing-dependent manner.
source: A further refinement of this approach was provided by patch-clamp recording, which revealed that strong electrical stimulation of even a single neuron can be detected in a cell-type and spike timing-dependent manner (Houweling and Brecht, 2008; Doron et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Houweling and Brecht, 2008; Doron et al., 2014.

claim: Single neuron stimulation can modulate behaviour in sensory-guided tasks.
source: to the extent that they can modulate behaviour in sensory-guided tasks (Tanke et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tanke et al., 2018.

claim: Strong stimulation of single pyramidal neurons in L2/3 recruits approximately 2% of local excitatory neurons.
source: Strong stimulation of single pyramidal neurons in L2/3 has been shown to recruit ~2% of local excitatory neurons and ~30% of local inhibitory neurons (Kwan and Dan, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kwan and Dan, 2012.

claim: Strong stimulation of single pyramidal neurons in L2/3 recruits approximately 30% of local inhibitory neurons.
source: Strong stimulation of single pyramidal neurons in L2/3 has been shown to recruit ~2% of local excitatory neurons and ~30% of local inhibitory neurons (Kwan and Dan, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kwan and Dan, 2012.

claim: A single pyramidal neuron spike in L5 is estimated to recruit approximately 28 post-synaptic neurons.
source: A single pyramidal neuron spike in L5 is estimated to recruit ~28 post-synaptic neurons (London et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to London et al., 2010.

claim: A single pyramidal neuron spike in L2/3 can trigger strong disynaptic inhibition.
source: and in L2/3 can trigger strong disynaptic inhibition (Jouhanneau et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jouhanneau et al., 2018.

claim: Single neurons can trigger global switches in brain state.
source: Single neurons can also trigger global switches in brain state (Li et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2009.

claim: Single neurons can influence network synchronisation.
source: influence network synchronisation (Bonifazi et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bonifazi et al., 2009.

claim: Single neurons can have a direct impact on motor output.
source: and have a direct impact on motor output (Brecht et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Brecht et al., 2004.

claim: Work investigating the impact of sparse activation on the local network in vivo has largely been done under anaesthesia.
source: However, work investigating the impact of sparse activation on the local network in vivo has largely been done under anaesthesia (London et al., 2010; Kwan and Dan, 2012; Jouhanneau et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to London et al., 2010; Kwan and Dan, 2012; Jouhanneau et al., 2018.

claim: Anaesthesia influences state-dependent cortical processing.
source: which influences state-dependent cortical processing (Niell and Stryker, 2010; Crochet et al., 2011; Harris and Thiele, 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Niell and Stryker, 2010; Crochet et al., 2011; Harris and Thiele, 2011.

claim: The lower bound for perception of cortical activity is approximately 14 pyramidal neurons.
source: By precisely titrating the number of neurons stimulated, we demonstrate that the lower bound for perception of cortical activity is ~14 pyramidal neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The relationship between the number of activated neurons and behaviour is a steep sigmoidal function.
source: We find a steep sigmoidal relationship between the number of activated neurons and behaviour, saturating at only ~37 neurons
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The psychometric relationship between activated neurons and behaviour saturates at approximately 37 neurons.
source: We find a steep sigmoidal relationship between the number of activated neurons and behaviour, saturating at only ~37 neurons
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The psychometric relationship between activated neurons and behaviour can shift with learning.
source: and show this relationship can shift with learning.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Activation of ensembles is balanced by inhibition of neighbouring neurons.
source: Furthermore, activation of ensembles is balanced by inhibition of neighbouring neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cortical perception balances a trade-off between minimizing the impact of noise while efficiently detecting relevant signals.
source: This surprising perceptual sensitivity in the face of potent network suppression supports the sparse coding hypothesis, and suggests that cortical perception balances a trade-off between minimizing the impact of noise while efficiently detecting relevant signals.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: GCaMP6s and C1V1 were expressed in neurons of L2/3 barrel cortex.
source: We expressed the calcium indicator GCaMP6s and the two-photon activatable somatically-restricted opsin C1V1 in neurons of L2/3 barrel cortex (Figure 1a: inset right, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, see Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by the methods described in the manuscript.

claim: The all-optical approach allows flexible activation of specific ensembles of neurons with high spatial resolution.
source: This strategy allows us to flexibly activate specific ensembles of neurons in a given cortical population (Figure 1a: Pixel STA, Figure 1—figure supplement 2) with high spatial resolution (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a: HWHM 5 µm laterally, 20 µm axially)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in figures.

claim: The lateral spatial resolution of two-photon photostimulation is 5 µm HWHM.
source: with high spatial resolution (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a: HWHM 5 µm laterally, 20 µm axially)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a.

claim: The axial spatial resolution of two-photon photostimulation is 20 µm HWHM.
source: with high spatial resolution (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a: HWHM 5 µm laterally, 20 µm axially)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Animals were trained to detect bulk activation of barrel cortex via 1P photostimulation.
source: Inspired by previous work (Histed and Maunsell, 2014; Huber et al., 2008) we devised a training paradigm in which animals were conditioned to detect bulk activation of barrel cortex via 1P photostimulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by the methods described in the manuscript.

claim: 1P stimulation intensity was progressively lowered during training.
source: After task acquisition, we progressively lowered the 1P stimulation intensity (which reduces the number, reliability and spatial extent of activated neurons (see Materials and methods for photostimulation details))
evidence: The claim is supported by the methods described in the manuscript.

claim: Animals were transitioned to detect 2P photostimulation of specific groups of neurons.
source: before transitioning animals to detect 2P photostimulation of specific groups of neurons (Figure 1b, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by the methods described in the manuscript and shown in figures.

claim: Animals detect 1P photostimulation and 2P stimulation targeted to 200 neurons to similar extents.
source: Animals detect 1P photostimulation and 2P stimulation targeted to 200 neurons to similar extents, at a level far above chance (catch trials), with similar reaction time mean and standard deviation.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1e-g.

claim: Animals detect 2P stimulation at a level far above chance.
source: Animals detect 1P photostimulation and 2P stimulation targeted to 200 neurons to similar extents, at a level far above chance (catch trials), with similar reaction time mean and standard deviation.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1e-g.

claim: Reaction times for 1P and 2P stimulation are similar.
source: Animals detect 1P photostimulation and 2P stimulation targeted to 200 neurons to similar extents, at a level far above chance (catch trials), with similar reaction time mean and standard deviation.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1f-g.

claim: Two-photon optogenetic stimulation targeted to small ensembles of cortical neurons can reliably drive behaviour.
source: Thus, we have demonstrated that two-photon optogenetic stimulation targeted to small ensembles of cortical neurons can reliably drive behaviour and provides a powerful tool for investigating the perceptual salience of different patterns of neural activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Animals' response rates increased sigmoidally with increasing numbers of target neurons activated.
source: Animals' response rates increased sigmoidally with increasing numbers of target neurons activated (Figure 2b single animal, Figure 2d all sessions)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2b and 2d.

claim: Individual sessions and aggregate data were well fit by log-normal sigmoid psychometric functions.
source: and both individual sessions and aggregate data across sessions were well fit by log-normal sigmoid psychometric functions (Figure 2d grey dots/lines: individual data/fits, R2 = 0.91 ± 0.09, N = 11 sessions, 6 mice, 1–2 sessions each; red line: aggregate fit, R2 = 0.72, cross-validated R2 = 0.67 ± 0.23, N = 10,000 permutations, see Materials and methods for fit details).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2d and statistical analysis.

claim: Animals can detect the activation of a minimum of approximately 14 neurons at their perceptual threshold.
source: Using these fitted psychometric functions, we estimate that animals can detect the activation of a minimum of ~14 neurons at their perceptual threshold (Figure 2d,e 10% point of curve: individual fits 14.2 ± 8.96 neurons, N = 11 sessions, 6 mice, 1–2 sessions each; aggregate fit 9.86 [95% CI: 6.09 12.8] neurons)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2d-e and statistical analysis.

claim: Approximately 37 neurons are required to saturate performance.
source: with only roughly double this number of neurons (~37) required to saturate performance (Figure 2d,e 90% point of curve: individual fits 37.0 ± 11.3 neurons, N = 11 sessions, 6 mice, 1–2 sessions each; aggregate fit 45.1 [95% CI: 37.3 63.5] neurons).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2d-e and statistical analysis.

claim: At the psychometric function's 50% point, approximately 0.05 probability of licking is added per neuron stimulated.
source: At the psychometric function's 50% point (Figure 2d,e 50% point of curve: individual fits 21.8 ± 8.71 neurons, N = 11 sessions, 6 mice, 1–2 sessions each; aggregate fit 21.1 [95% CI: 17.9 23.9] neurons) this results in a very steep slope, with ~0.05 probability of licking added per neuron stimulated (Figure 2f individual fits 0.05 ± 0.03; aggregate fit 0.03).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2f and statistical analysis.

claim: Mean reaction times did not vary as fewer neurons were activated.
source: Mean reaction times did not vary as fewer neurons were activated (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a β = −0.02, R2 = 0.02, p=0.24)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a and statistical analysis.

claim: Reaction times became more variable as fewer neurons were activated.
source: although they did become more variable (Figure 2—figure supplement 2b β = −0.05, R2 = 0.30, p=1.41 × 10−6).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2b and statistical analysis.

claim: There was a consistent improvement in detection rate across sessions.
source: Across all animals there was a consistent improvement in detection rate (Figure 2—figure supplement 3c P(Lick) on Session 1: 0.17 ± 0.18 vs Session 2: 0.28 ± 0.25, p=6.29 × 10−3 paired t-test, N = 14 mice testing the same 30 neurons and 5 mice testing different groups of 25 and 50 neurons)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3c and statistical analysis.

claim: Improvement in detection rate did not differ depending on whether the same or different neurons were stimulated across sessions.
source: which did not differ depending on whether the same or different neurons were stimulated across sessions (Figure 2—figure supplement 3d P(Lick) improvement for same: 0.12 ± 0.18 vs different: 0.09 ± 0.18, p=0.84 Mann Whitney U-Test, N = 14 mice testing the same 30 neurons and 5 mice testing different groups of 25 and 50 neurons).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3d and statistical analysis.

claim: Hits were associated with more activation than misses.
source: Splitting trials by hits and misses we found that hits were associated with more activation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a,b P(activated) background on hits 4.94 × 10−2 ± 8.63 x 10−3 vs misses 3.83 × 10−2 ± 5.04 x 10−3 on 50 target trials, p=1.95 × 10−3 Wilcoxon signed-rank test, N = 11 sessions, 6 mice, 1–2 sessions each)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a-b and statistical analysis.

claim: Hits were associated with less suppression than misses.
source: and less suppression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1e,f P(suppressed) background on hits 3.53 × 10−2 ± 4.84 x 10−3 vs misses 3.99 × 10−2 ± 5.5 x 10−3 on 50 target trials, p=2.23 × 10−2 paired t-test, N = 11 sessions, 6 mice, 1–2 sessions each) than misses.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1e-f and statistical analysis.

claim: The level of activation recruited on hits post-photostimulation was not different from false alarms on catch trials.
source: Indeed we found that in background neurons the level of activation recruited on hits post-photostimulation was not different from false alarms on catch trials where animals licked but no neurons were photostimulated (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d P(activated) background on 50 target hit 4.92 × 10−2 ± 9.05 x 10−3 vs catch false alarm 4.83 × 10−2 ± 1.04 x 10−2, p=0.52 paired t-test, N = 10 sessions, 6 mice, 1–2 sessions each, 1 session without any catch false alarms excluded)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1d and statistical analysis.

claim: A large fraction of neurons showed activity which was modulated by spontaneous licking.
source: In line with this, we found that a large fraction of neurons showed activity which was modulated by spontaneous licking (Figure 3—figure supplement 1i–k 46% ± 11 of neurons lick modulated, N = 11 sessions, 6 mice, 1–2 sessions each, see Materials and methods)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1i-k and statistical analysis.

claim: Photostimulation causes both activation and suppression in the network.
source: Taking the network as a whole (including target neurons), we found that photostimulation causes both activation (Figure 3a right inset; P(activated) all neurons on photostimulus 5.91 × 10−2 ± 1.20 x 10−2 vs catch 4.82 × 10−2 ± 6.65 x 10−3 trials averaged across all trial types, p=1.17 × 10−3 paired t-test, N = 10 sessions, 6 mice, 1–2 sessions each) and suppression (Figure 3b right inset; P(suppressed) all neurons on photostimulus 4.58 × 10−2 ± 4.90 x 10−3 vs catch 3.97 × 10−2 ± 4.80 x 10−3 trials averaged across all trial types, p=1.41 × 10−4 paired t-test, N = 10 sessions, 6 mice, 1–2 sessions each)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3a-b and statistical analysis.

claim: Both activation and suppression scale with the number of neurons activated.
source: and that both scale with the number of neurons activated (Figure 3a,b P(activated) all neurons: β = 7.54 × 10−3, R2 = 0.24, p=2.36 × 10−5; P(suppressed) all neurons: β = 3.00 × 10−3, R2 = 0.25, p=1.54 × 10−5, N = 10 sessions, 6 mice, 1–2 sessions each).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3a-b and statistical analysis.

claim: Only background network suppression scales with the number of activated target neurons.
source: When we analysed only background neurons (i.e. excluding targets from the calculation), we found that while photostimulation does cause both activation and suppression in the background network (Figure 3d,e right insets; P(activated) network on photostimulus 4.40 × 10−2 ± 6.89 x 10−3 vs catch 4.02 × 10−2 ± 5.60 x 10−3 trials, p=2.31 × 10−3 paired t-test; P(suppressed) background on photostimulation 3.81 × 10−2 ± 4.60 x 10−3 vs catch 3.27 × 10−2 ± 4.60 x 10−3 trials, p=1.06 × 10−4 paired t-test, all averaged across trial types, N = 10 sessions, 6 mice, 1–2 sessions each), only background network suppression scales with the number of activated target neurons (Figure 3e β = 2.95 × 10−3, R2 = 0.31, p=7.79 × 10−7), whereas activation does not (Figure 3d β = 1.70 × 10−3, R2 = 0.05, p=0.08).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3d-e and statistical analysis.

claim: There is a consistent balance of activation and suppression across all target activation levels.
source: Indeed, across all neurons in the population we see that there is a consistent balance of activation and suppression across all target activation levels (Figure 3c P(Activated)/P(Suppressed) across all neurons β = 7.23 × 10−2, R2 = 0.05, p=0.06)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3c and statistical analysis.

claim: The ratio of activation to suppression remains similar to the rates observed spontaneously during catch trials.
source: that remains similar to the rates observed spontaneously during catch trials (Figure 3c right inset; P(Activated)/P(Suppressed) on photostimulation 1.30 ± 0.28 vs catch 1.24 ± 0.25 trials across all neurons, p=0.25 paired t-test, N = 10 sessions, 6 mice, 1–2 sessions each).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3c and statistical analysis.

claim: Target neuron activation is the strongest and most generalisable predictor of behavioural responses.
source: The strongest and most generalisable predictor of behavioural responses was target neuron activation, which had significantly positive R2 across both training and test sets during cross-validation (Figure 4a,d train R2: 0.71 ± 0.06, p=0 permutation test vs 0; test R2: 0.66 ± 0.23, p=1.68 × 10−2 permutation test vs 0, N = 10,000 train:test splits).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4a,d and statistical analysis.

claim: Network suppression had mild predictive power on training data, but none on testing data.
source: Network suppression had mild predictive power on training data, but none on testing data (Figure 4c,d train R2: 0.16 ± 0.06, p=2.50 × 10−3 permutation test vs 0; test R2: 0.01 ± 0.39, p=0.39 permutation test vs 0, N = 10,000 train:test splits)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4c-d and statistical analysis.

claim: Network activation was a poor predictor of both training and testing data.
source: Network activation was a poor predictor of both training and testing data, suggesting that it had little influence on behavioural performance (Figure 4b,d train R2: −0.05 ± 0.05, p=0.11 permutation test vs 0; test R2: −0.21 ± 0.44, p=0.22 permutation test vs 0, N = 10,000 train:test splits).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4b,d and statistical analysis.

claim: The perceptual threshold measured is remarkably low at approximately 14 cortical neurons.
source: The perceptual threshold we measured is remarkably low: mice can detect the activation of only ~14 cortical neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The perceptual threshold is substantially lower than the threshold estimated for one-photon activation of layer 2/3 neurons in rodent barrel cortex.
source: This number is substantially lower than the threshold estimated for one-photon activation of layer 2/3 neurons in rodent barrel cortex (~60; Huber et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with data from Huber et al., 2008.

claim: The minimum threshold of approximately 140 action potentials is lower than the approximately 300 reported by Huber et al.
source: Moreover, our stimuli drive double the number of action potentials (~10 in each neuron) which Huber et al. show increases detectability, though we note that our minimum threshold of ~140 action potentials (10 action potentials in 14 neurons) is still lower than the ~300 that they report.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with data from Huber et al., 2008.

claim: The reaction times to optogenetic stimuli are comparable to, although slightly slower than, those reported for detection of whisker stimuli in mice.
source: Interestingly, the reaction times to optogenetic stimuli that we report (0.4–0.7 s) are comparable to, although slightly slower than, those reported for detection of whisker stimuli in mice (0.3–0.4 s; Chen et al., 2013a; Hires et al., 2015; O'Connor et al., 2010; Sachidhanandam et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with data from multiple cited studies.

claim: The perceptual threshold of approximately 14 neurons could be important for avoiding perceptual false positives caused by spontaneous background network activity.
source: The threshold of ~14 neurons could therefore be important for avoiding perceptual false positives caused by spontaneous background network activity.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: The relatively low perceptual threshold may have significant computational advantages.
source: The relatively low perceptual threshold may also have significant computational advantages.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: The demonstration that the perceptual threshold is much lower than the dimensionality of barrel cortex but significantly higher than a single neuron is consistent with computational theories proposing sparse coding.
source: Our demonstration that the perceptual threshold (~14 neurons) is much lower than the dimensionality of barrel cortex (~400,000 neurons in barrel cortex; Hooks et al., 2011; Meyer et al., 2013; ~2000 neurons in superficial layers of a barrel; Lefort et al., 2009), but also significantly higher than a single neuron, is consistent with computational theories proposing that individual items are represented sparsely compared to the dimensionality of the space, but also that they are not represented by single elements of that space (Baum et al., 1988; Kanerva, 1993; Olshausen and Field, 2004; Palm, 1980).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results and comparison with computational theories.

claim: The network input-output function for perception is sigmoidal and remarkably steep.
source: This function is sigmoidal and remarkably steep, saturating at only ~37 neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The steep input-output function may have significant functional consequences.
source: This steep input-output function may have significant functional consequences.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: The steep input-output function enables perceptual detection of relevant activity with high sensitivity and efficiency.
source: While allowing rejection of noise due to spontaneous activity (see the previous section), it also enables perceptual detection of relevant activity with high sensitivity and efficiency, and yet avoids further unnecessary engagement of the network with additional stimulation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: The steepness of the input-output function and the low number of neurons at saturation are consistent with optimal energy efficiency.
source: The steepness of the input-output function and the low number of neurons at saturation are also consistent with optimal energy efficiency (Attwell and Laughlin, 2001; Lennie, 2003).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results and comparison with cited studies.

claim: The perceptual threshold is not fixed and depends on learning in a neuron-agnostic manner.
source: We have used our ability to specifically target the same (or different) neurons across multiple days to show that the perceptual threshold is not fixed and depends on learning in a neuron-agnostic manner.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The learning observed during the 2P training phase generalises to neurons that are not stimulated during this period.
source: The fact that the learning we observe during the 2P training phase generalises to neurons that are not stimulated during this period suggests that animals can 'learn to learn' (Harlow, 1949) within the context of detecting arbitrary cortical activity patterns
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The matched suppression observed in the local L2/3 network is in accordance with the general net inhibitory effect of pyramidal neuron stimulation observed in vivo.
source: The matched suppression that we observed in the local L2/3 network is in accordance with the general net inhibitory effect of pyramidal neuron stimulation observed in vivo (Chettih and Harvey, 2019; Kwan and Dan, 2012; Mateo et al., 2011; Russell et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and comparison with cited studies.

claim: The results support the idea that cortical networks operate in an inhibition-stabilised regime.
source: This supports the idea that such networks operate in an inhibition-stabilised regime where one role of inhibition is to control strong recurrent excitation (Denève and Machens, 2016; Murphy and Miller, 2009; Ozeki et al., 2009; Pehlevan and Sompolinsky, 2014; Sanzeni et al., 2020; Tsodyks et al., 1997; van Vreeswijk and Sompolinsky, 1996; Wolf et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results and comparison with cited studies.

claim: All experimental procedures were carried out under Project Licence 70/14018 (PCC4A4ECE) issued by the UK Home Office.
source: All experimental procedures were carried out under Project Licence 70/14018 (PCC4A4ECE) issued by the UK Home Office in accordance with the UK Animals (Scientific Procedures) Act (1986) and were also subject to local ethical review.
evidence: The claim is a statement of regulatory compliance.

claim: 4–6 week old wild-type (C57/BL6) and transgenic GCaMP6s mice of both sexes were used.
source: 4–6 week old wild-type (C57/BL6) and transgenic GCaMP6s mice (Emx1-Cre;CaMKIIa-tTA;Ai94) of both sexes were used.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental subjects.

claim: Two-photon imaging was performed using a resonant scanning (30 Hz) microscope driven by PrairieView and a Chameleon Ultra II laser.
source: For most experiments (Figure 2, 3 and 4) two-photon imaging was performed using a resonant scanning (30 Hz) microscope (Ultima II, Bruker Corporation) driven by PrairieView and a Chameleon Ultra II laser (Coherent).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methods.

claim: Two-photon photostimulation was carried out using a femto-second pulsed laser at 1030 nm.
source: Two-photon photostimulation was carried out using a femto-second pulsed laser at 1030 nm (Satsuma, Amplitude Systèmes, 2 MHz rep-rate, 20 W).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methods.

claim: Each spiral consisted of three rotations, 10 μm diameter, 20 ms duration.
source: Each spiral consisted of three rotations (i.e. from centre to edge of spiral), 10 μm diameter, 20 ms duration.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methods.

claim: Powers were adjusted to maintain 6 mW per target neuron.
source: Powers were adjusted to maintain 6 mW per target neuron.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methods.

claim: All 2P stimuli should drive approximately 10 action potentials.
source: From our previous work, we expect a single spiral to produce ~1 action potential (Packer et al., 2015), thus all 2P stimuli should drive ~10 action potentials.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from previous work cited.

claim: All LED stimuli consisted of 5 × 20 ms pulses at 25 Hz of varying powers ranging from 10 to 0.02 mW.
source: All LED stimuli consisted of 5 × 20 ms pulses at 25 Hz of varying powers ranging from 10 to 0.02 mW (measured with PM100A power meter/S130C photodiode sensor, ThorLabs).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methods.
